t: Reformat Date — String Parsing and Zero-Padding
o:
We are given a date string like "20th Oct 2052" and must output "2052-10-20": year first, then a two-digit month, then a two-digit day. The input has three space-separated tokens: day (number plus ordinal suffix), three-letter month abbreviation, and four-digit year.

**Example walkthroughs:**
- "20th Oct 2052": strip "th" from "20th" to get 20; "Oct" maps to month 10; year is 2052 → "2052-10-20".
- "6th Jun 1933": day 6 needs zero-padding to "06"; "Jun" → 06; result "1933-06-06".
- "26th May 1960": day 26, month 05, year 1960 → "1960-05-26".

**Constraints implications:** Input is guaranteed valid and tiny (one short string), so any straightforward parsing works. The only real work is (1) removing the ordinal suffix from the day, (2) mapping the month abbreviation to its number, and (3) zero-padding the day and month to two digits.
k: Splitting on spaces cleanly separates day, month, and year tokens.
The ordinal suffix can be removed by stripping the last two characters of the day token.
A fixed array of 12 month abbreviations gives an O(1) index lookup for the month number.
Zero-padding to width 2 handles single-digit days/months uniformly.

a.i: Split the string into its three tokens. The day number is the day token minus its last two characters (the suffix). Look up the month's index in a hardcoded list of abbreviations (index + 1 = month number). Format with zero-padding: year as-is, month and day padded to two digits.
s: Split the date string on spaces into [dayToken, monthToken, year].
Day = integer value of dayToken without its last two characters.
Month = index of monthToken in ["Jan",...,"Dec"] plus 1.
a.t: O(1) — the string has bounded length; splitting and one linear scan of 12 months are constant work.
a.sp: O(1) — only a few small temporary strings/arrays of fixed size.

a.i: Avoid library splitting/formatting by scanning the string manually: read digits until a non-digit for the day, skip the suffix and space, match the next three letters against the month table, then take the remaining four characters as the year. This shows you understand the format at the character level and avoids regex/split dependencies.
s: Scan leading digits to build the day number.
Skip the two-letter ordinal suffix and the following space.
Read three letters and find their position in the month abbreviation array.
Take the remaining four characters as the year string.
Assemble YYYY-MM-DD with manual zero-padding ('0' prefix when < 10).

c.python:
class Solution:
    def reformatDate(self, date: str) -> str:
        months = ["Jan","Feb","Mar","Apr","May","Jun","Jul","Aug","Sep","Oct","Nov","Dec"]
        i = 0
        day = 0
        while date[i].isdigit():
            day = day * 10 + int(date[i]); i += 1
        i += 3  # skip suffix and space
        mon = months.index(date[i:i+3]) + 1
        year = date[i+4:]
        return f"{year}-{mon:02d}-{day:02d}"

a.t: O(1) — a single pass over a fixed-length string.

w:
**Which approach to pick:** In an interview, go straight to Approach 1 — split, map via a month array, and pad. It is the clearest and shortest correct solution; Approach 2 is worth mentioning only if asked to avoid library helpers or if the interviewer probes lower-level parsing.

**Common pitfalls:**
- Forgetting to zero-pad single-digit days and months (e.g., "6th Jun 1933" → "1933-6-6" is wrong).
- Assuming the day always has two digits before the suffix — it can be one digit ("1st"–"9th").
- Off-by-one in the month mapping (array index vs. 1-based month number).
- In Java/C++, forgetting that `split`/`stringstream` handle multiple spaces differently than expected (not an issue here since input is well-formed).

**Edge cases:** days 1–9 (padding), all twelve months, years at both ends (1900, 2100). No invalid inputs need handling per constraints.

**Follow-ups:** parse dates with full month names or different locales; validate dates instead of trusting input; reformat to other standards (e.g., ISO 8601 with time); batch-convert many dates efficiently.
